requirement: In a book chapter, each valid `{impl}`, `{cite}`, or `{test}` reference, inline or fenced, MUST render as a Shields.io static badge image with meaningful alt text that displays its role and full name and links to the badge at the corresponding `{req}` or `{example}` definition. Links MUST work across chapters, including nested chapters. A fenced reference MUST render its badge followed by its body as Markdown. Each fenced `{req}` or `{example}` directive MUST render as a Shields.io definition badge image identifying its kind; text outside a directive MUST remain literal. Badge text MUST remain legible regardless of whether its link has been visited. A badge link MUST show a visible indicator when it has keyboard focus and MAY brighten on hover. These badges use the syntax defined by {cite}`requirements.references.targets`.
rationale: **Verdict:** the Rust rendering logic is largely complete and well tested. Two gaps remain in the CSS part of the requirement, and neither is acknowledged by a FIXME, so the judgment is false. **What the Rust code does and how it is tested** - Reference badges: - `shield_badge`, `reference_badge`, `replace_inline_references` and `replace_references` (src/lib.rs) render each valid `{impl}`, `{cite}` and `{test}` reference as a Shields.io static ``. - The alt text is "role name", and the badge links to `#habeas--` at the definition. - `chapter_href` computes `../` prefixes for nested chapters. - `DefinitionKind::badge`/`anchor` and `ReferenceKind::label`/`color` supply the kind labels, anchors and colours. - Fenced references: - `fenced::markdown_fences` (src/fenced.rs) finds the fences. - `replace_references` emits the badge followed by the recursively rendered body. - Definition badges: - `replace_definitions` renders fenced `{req}` and `{example}` directives as definition badges with kind labels `req` and `example`. - It leaves invalid or unclosed directives, code examples and legacy inline roles literal. - Tests: - `references_in_nested_chapters_link_to_the_requirement_definition` covers all three roles and the `../` link from `guides/deep.md`. - `fenced_references_render_their_badge_and_body_and_built_ins_are_unlinked` covers fenced order, alt text, and literal unknown names, inline built-ins and code fences. - `shields_badge_urls_escape_requirement_names` covers badge URL and alt text. - `colon_directives_render_markdown_bodies_and_legacy_roles_stay_literal` covers definition badges and literal text. - `examples_are_distinct_definitions_and_tests_link_to_them` covers example badges and links to examples. **Gaps** 1. **No test covers the CSS obligations.** - Three obligations live only in `md/habeas.css`: legibility when visited (`a.habeas-req-badge:visited`), the keyboard-focus indicator (`:focus-visible` outline), and the optional hover brighten. - No test or other check verifies that the shipped stylesheet contains them. - `tests/setup.rs` only checks that the stylesheet is copied. - A browser-level test would be impractical, but a simple check of the stylesheet is cheap. The "MUST show a visible indicator when it has keyboard focus" obligation therefore has no verification at all. 2. **The anchored `{impl}` stylesheet contains behaviour the requirement does not specify.** - `.habeas-fenced-ref` adds a purple left border, margin and padding to every fenced reference. - `.habeas-builtin` sets `cursor: help`. - `.habeas-req-badge` and `.habeas-shield` set layout rules. - `audits/requirement-rewordings/ci-references-definitions.md` shows the project previously treated unspecified stylesheet behaviour as a gap. It either moved the rule out or reworded the requirement. - The fenced-reference border and padding are end-user-visible and are neither specified nor covered by another requirement. Both gaps would be easy to close: add a stylesheet test, and either specify or drop the extra decoration.

text: In a book chapter, each valid `{impl}`, `{cite}`, or `{test}` reference, inline or fenced, MUST render as a Shields.io static badge image with meaningful alt text that displays its role and full name and links to the badge at the corresponding `{req}` or `{example}` definition. Links MUST work across chapters, including nested chapters. A fenced reference MUST render its badge followed by its body as Markdown. Each fenced `{req}` or `{example}` directive MUST render as a Shields.io definition badge image identifying its kind; text outside a directive MUST remain literal. Badge text MUST remain legible regardless of whether its link has been visited. A badge link MUST show a visible indicator when it has keyboard focus and MAY brighten on hover. These badges use the syntax defined by {cite}`requirements.references.targets`.

Project text files MAY use the `{impl}`, `{cite}`, and `{test}` roles with a backtick-delimited full requirement or example name, or with a built-in name under {cite}`requirements.references.builtin_definitions`. A reference MAY instead be written in fenced form, `:::{role} name` on one line, a body, and a closing fence, following the fence rules of {cite}`requirements.ci.span` and {cite}`requirements.ci.fence_lengths`; the fenced form is the same edge with attached commentary, and the inline form carries none. In a source comment, fence lines MUST be recognized after removing each line's comment delimiters within one comment run under {cite}`requirements.references.outline_comments`, and a fence that does not close within its comment run MUST be a validation error. Each reference is a directed edge between its source and the named definition. A source is a project source item or a requirement or example declaration. `{cite}` MUST mean that the source relies on, supports, or refers to the definition, and is an edge from the source to the definition. `{impl}` MUST mean that the source implements part of the definition: it makes a decision, performs a check, produces an output, or handles a case that the definition specifies. A requirement MAY implement part of another requirement by refining one of its obligations. Calling code that implements a definition, or producing a result a caller uses to meet it, MUST NOT by itself count as implementing it. A requirement stating a convention for every output of a kind, such as every validation error, is implemented by the source that carries out the convention as a whole, such as the step that collects and reports those outputs. `{test}` MUST mean that the source is designed to verify behavior the definition specifies: a test through its scenario and the assertions about that scenario's outcome, or a named example through the concrete case it describes. `{impl}` and `{test}` are edges from the definition to the source. Only requirements and examples are assessed; code is reviewed as part of the definitions it implements or tests. Habeas MUST find these references throughout project source files and MUST fail with the source file and line if a name has no matching `{req}` or `{example}` definition. In Markdown, escaped roles and roles in code examples MUST remain literal. Evidence snapshots and generated build output MUST NOT be counted as additional source references: discovery MUST skip `.git` and `target` directories at any depth and the project-root `book` and `evidence` directories.
